claims.statement: Kumanokusubi is a deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Kumanokusubi adalah dewa dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Kumanokusubi (熊野久须毘命,熊野櫲樟日命, Wonder Worker of Bear Moors) is a God in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: The tradition counts him as Amaterasu’s fifth son.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi menghitungnya sebagai putra kelima Amaterasu.
claims.quote: He is the fifth son of Amaterasu.

claims.statement: His birth belongs to a contest between Amaterasu and Susanoo.
claims.statement_id: Kelahirannya merupakan bagian dari perlombaan antara Amaterasu dan Susanoo.
claims.quote: He was born out of a kami-making competition between Amaterasu and Susanoo.

claims.statement: One version describes five male kami arising from chewed beads.
claims.statement_id: Satu versi menggambarkan lima kami laki-laki lahir dari manik-manik yang dikunyah.
claims.quote: In many versions, Susanoo took Amaterasu's beads and crushed them within his mouth, which created five male kami.

claims.statement: The Kojiki connects his emergence with the jeweled cord on Amaterasu’s right wrist.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menghubungkan kemunculannya dengan untaian permata di pergelangan kanan Amaterasu.
claims.quote: Then he asked for the jeweled [cord] adorning her right wrist, and [she] handed it over [to him]. He chewed it up and spat the bits out in a misty spray from which a deity named Kumanokusubi no mikoto 熊野久湏毗命 came into existence (15).

claims.statement: The birth narrative describes the chewed material being spat out as a misty spray.
claims.statement_id: Narasi kelahiran menggambarkan bahan yang dikunyah diludahkan sebagai semburan berkabut.
claims.quote: Then he asked for the jeweled [cord] adorning her right wrist, and [she] handed it over [to him]. He chewed it up and spat the bits out in a misty spray from which a deity named Kumanokusubi no mikoto 熊野久湏毗命 came into existence (15).

claims.statement: Kussie is a lake cryptid associated with Lake Kussharo in Hokkaidō.
claims.statement_id: Kussie adalah kriptid danau yang dikaitkan dengan Danau Kussharo di Hokkaidō.
claims.quote: Kussie ... is a Japanese lake monster (a cryptid) said to be living in Hokkaidō's Lake Kussharo on the northern island of Hokkaido.

claims.statement: Its nickname is associated with the name Nessie.
claims.statement_id: Julukannya dikaitkan dengan nama Nessie.
claims.quote: The name "Kussie" is ostensibly inspired by "Nessie", the nickname for the Loch Ness Monster in Scotland.

claims.statement: The lake lies in the eastern part of Hokkaidō.
claims.statement_id: Danau tersebut berada di bagian timur Hokkaidō.
claims.quote: Lake Kussharo, where Kussie is said to live, is situated within Akan National Park in eastern Hokkaido.

claims.statement: A lakeside statue represents the creature.
claims.statement_id: Patung di tepi danau menggambarkan makhluk itu.
claims.quote: A statue of Kussie on the shore of Lake Kussharo signifies the figure's prominence in local culture.

claims.statement: Lake Kussharo is a caldera lake, meaning it was formed in the crater of a volcano.
claims.statement_id: Danau Kussharo adalah danau kaldera, yaitu danau yang terbentuk di kawah gunung berapi.
claims.quote: Lake Kussharo ... The lake is a caldera lake, meaning it was formed in the crater of a volcano.

claims.statement: The name of Lake Kussharo derives from the Ainu word "Kuccharo", translated as "The place where a lake becomes a river and the river flows out".
claims.statement_id: Nama Danau Kussharo berasal dari kata Ainu "Kuccharo", yang diterjemahkan sebagai "tempat danau menjadi sungai dan sungai mengalir keluar".
claims.quote: Lake Kussharo ... This lake is notable for its connection to Ainu culture, as its name derives from the Ainu word "Kuccharo", which translates to "The place where a lake becomes a river and the river flows out".

claims.statement: Stories about Kussie are said to contribute to local folklore and to attract curiosity and tourism to the area.
claims.statement_id: Cerita tentang Kussie disebut menambah cerita rakyat setempat serta menarik rasa ingin tahu dan wisatawan ke kawasan itu.
claims.quote: Similar to other lake monster tales around the world, stories about Kussie contribute to local folklore and attract curiosity and tourism to the area.

claims.statement: A government tourism text spells the name Kusshi and says it is said to reside in Lake Kussharo, a caldera lake in Hokkaido.
claims.statement_id: Teks pariwisata resmi pemerintah ini menulis namanya Kusshi dan menyebut makhluk itu konon tinggal di Danau Kussharo, danau kaldera di Hokkaido.
claims.quote: The legendary local monster Isshi met Kusshi, who is said to reside in Lake Kussharo, a caldera lake in Hokkaido, Japan’s northernmost prefecture.

claims.statement: In 1983, Kusshi and the lake creature Isshi were brought together on Lake Ikeda in an event described as a meeting of Japan's two most famous legendary lake creatures.
claims.statement_id: Pada 1983, Kusshi dan makhluk danau Isshi dipertemukan di Danau Ikeda dalam acara yang digambarkan sebagai pertemuan dua makhluk danau legendaris paling terkenal di Jepang.
claims.quote: In 1983, Japan’s two most famous legendary lake creatures met on the waters of Lake Ikeda. The legendary local monster Isshi met Kusshi

claims.statement: Approximately 3,000 spectators watched large models of Isshi and Kusshi tour the lake together on a raft.
claims.statement_id: Kira-kira 3.000 penonton menyaksikan model besar Isshi dan Kusshi berkeliling danau bersama di atas rakit.
claims.quote: Approximately 3,000 spectators, as well as renowned manga artists such as Tezuka Osamu, watched large models of Isshi and Kusshi leisurely tour the lake together on a raft drifting through fog created by dry ice.

claims.statement: Mintuci is a water spirit in Ainu mythology and folklore.
claims.statement_id: Mintuci adalah roh air dalam mitologi dan cerita rakyat Ainu.
claims.quote: The mintuci (Ainu ミントゥチ; also mintuci kamuy, also transliterated into Japanese as mintsuchi (ミンツチ)) is a water sprite or an aquatic supernatural creature, a half-man-half-beast, told in stories of Ainu mythology and folklore.

claims.statement: It is described as a half-man-half-beast creature.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan sebagai makhluk setengah manusia setengah hewan (half-man-half-beast).
claims.quote: a water sprite or an aquatic supernatural creature, a half-man-half-beast, told in stories of Ainu mythology and folklore.

claims.statement: Some accounts relate it to the kappa.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian kisah menghubungkannya dengan kappa.
claims.quote: It is also considered a variant of the kappa and, therefore, a type of yōkai.

claims.statement: Japanese folklore studies also use the spelling mintsuchi.
claims.statement_id: Kajian cerita rakyat berbahasa Jepang juga memakai ejaan mintsuchi.
claims.quote: The name is mintuci (Ainu: ミントゥチ) according to modern Ainu orthography, but it is also commonly spelled mintsuchi (ミンツチ) in folkloric study literature written in Japanese.

claims.statement: An early dictionary locates the creature in lakes and rivers.
claims.statement_id: Kamus awal menempatkan makhluk ini di danau dan sungai.
claims.quote: The mintuci has been defined as "fabulous animal", purported to be "half human and half animal and to inhabit lakes and rivers" in the Ainu dictionary c. 1900 compiled by British missionary John Batchelor.

claims.statement: One explanation links its name with the Japanese term mizuchi.
claims.statement_id: Satu penjelasan menghubungkan namanya dengan istilah Jepang mizuchi.
claims.quote: The Ainu word mintuci is considered to be borrowed from the Japanese word mizuchi (or variants thereof), that are local appellations for the kappa, ultimately deriving from the term mizuchi, which signifies a type of dragon.

claims.statement: The mintuci are said to hunt people and livestock by dragging them underwater, a trait also often ascribed to the kappa.
claims.statement_id: Mintuci konon memburu manusia dan ternak dengan menyeretnya ke dalam air, sifat yang juga sering dikaitkan dengan kappa.
claims.quote: The mintuci are said to hunt people and livestock by dragging them underwater, but this prankishness is also a trait frequently ascribed to the kappa

claims.statement: The mintuci are reputed to be of the height and stature of a human child of 3 to 12 or 13 years.
claims.statement_id: Mintuci dikabarkan setinggi dan sebesar anak manusia berumur 3 hingga 12 atau 13 tahun.
claims.quote: The mintuci are reputed to be of the height and stature of a 3-year-old to a 12-year-old or 13-year-old human.

claims.statement: The mintuci's skin is described as purplish or reddish with a sea turtle-like texture, and it has either bird-like feet or four sets of hooves.
claims.statement_id: Kulit mintuci digambarkan keunguan atau kemerahan dengan tekstur seperti kulit penyu laut, dan kakinya seperti kaki burung atau berupa empat set kuku.
claims.quote: The mintuci ... Its skin is purplish or reddish, with sea turtle-like texture, and they have either bird-like feet or four sets of hooves, with one supposed witness discovering sickle-like footprints.

claims.statement: The mintuci is generally considered an evil-dispositioned aquatic creature, but there are also benevolent types called pirika mintuci that inhabit the mountains.
claims.statement_id: Mintuci umumnya dianggap makhluk air yang berwatak jahat, tetapi ada pula jenis baik bernama pirika mintuci yang menghuni pegunungan.
claims.quote: Although the mintuci is generally considered an "evil dispositioned" type of fabulous aquatic creature, reputed to "disembowel and devour human beings when they catch them", there are also benevolent types called pirika mintuci (lit. "good mintuci") which inhabit the mountains according to John Batchelor.

claims.statement: Because the mintuci is regarded as a deity controlling fish, it may bring luck to fishermen, but at the price of more deaths by drowning.
claims.statement_id: Karena mintuci dianggap dewa yang menguasai ikan, ia dapat membawa keberuntungan bagi nelayan, tetapi dengan harga berupa bertambahnya kematian akibat tenggelam.
claims.quote: As the mintuci is a deity which controls the fish, it may bring luck to fishermen, but at a price, because as long as it is present, it will be responsible for an increase in deaths by drowning.

claims.statement: According to folk tradition, the mintuci also blesses hunters with plentiful game.
claims.statement_id: Menurut tradisi rakyat, mintuci juga memberkati pemburu dengan hasil buruan yang melimpah.
claims.quote: The mintuci also blesses the hunter, rewarding him with game in plenitude according to folk tradition.

claims.statement: The mintuci is thought capable of turning into a youth and becoming an adopted husband in a home with only daughters, bringing hunting luck, but if the village incurs his wrath he leaves with the community's food spirit, causing famine.
claims.statement_id: Mintuci diyakini dapat berubah menjadi pemuda dan menjadi menantu angkat di rumah yang hanya punya anak perempuan serta membawa keberuntungan berburu, tetapi bila desa membangkitkan amarahnya ia pergi membawa roh pangan komunitas sehingga terjadi kelaparan.
claims.quote: The mintuci is thought capable of transforming into a youth and becoming an adopted husband at a home with only daughters, bringing about fortune and luck of the hunt, but once the village incurs his wrath, he will depart, absconding with the community's food spirit, causing famine.

claims.statement: According to one origin myth, the puppets that drowned in the fight against the smallpox demon thereafter became the mintuci kamuy, who help people in illness or adversity.
claims.statement_id: Menurut satu mitos asal-usul, boneka-boneka yang tenggelam setelah melawan setan cacar kemudian menjadi mintuci kamuy yang menolong manusia saat sakit atau kesulitan.
claims.quote: All but one of the puppets drowned, and the grand general who remained managed to defeat the smallpox demon. The puppets that drowned thereafter became the mintuci kamuy, helping people in case of illness or adversity.

claims.statement: According to some Ainu elders, mintuci was a name people on the Japanese mainland used for the kappa, and the correct Ainu term was Shiri-sham-ainu, literally a "mountain-side-person".
claims.statement_id: Menurut sebagian tetua Ainu, mintuci adalah nama yang dipakai orang di daratan utama Jepang untuk kappa, dan istilah Ainu yang tepat adalah Shiri-sham-ainu, secara harfiah "orang di lereng gunung".
claims.quote: According to some Ainu elders, mintuci was a name that people on the Japanese mainland used to refer to kappa, and the correct Ainu term was Shiri-sham-ainu (シリシャマイヌ), literally denoting a "mountain-side-person".

claims.statement: The name varies by locality: mimtuci in the Chitose dialect and mintoci in the Ishikari region.
claims.statement_id: Namanya bervariasi menurut daerah: mimtuci dalam dialek Chitose dan mintoci di wilayah Ishikari.
claims.quote: The name manifests local variation, and the creature is called mimtuci (ミムトゥチ) in the Chitose dialect and mintoci (ミントチ) in the Ishikari region.

claims.statement: In the Tokachi and "Kurshiro" (the source's spelling) regions the creature is known as hundoci or slight variants of it.
claims.statement_id: Di wilayah Tokachi dan "Kurshiro" (ejaan sumber), makhluk ini dikenal dengan nama hundoci atau variannya.
claims.quote: The creature is known by the name hundoci (フンドチ) or slight variants thereof in the Tokachi and Kurshiro regions.

claims.statement: People may become possessed by the mintuci, and women possessed by one may try to seduce men.
claims.statement_id: Orang dapat dirasuki mintuci, dan perempuan yang dirasuki konon dapat mencoba menggoda laki-laki.
claims.quote: People may also become possessed by the mintuci, and women possessed by one may attempt to seduce men.

claims.statement: Batchelor gave a strictly Ainu etymology: a compound of mimi (or mim) 'flesh' and tumunci 'devil'.
claims.statement_id: Batchelor memberi etimologi yang murni Ainu: gabungan mimi (atau mim) 'daging' dan tumunci 'setan'.
claims.quote: However, Batchelor has given a strictly Ainu etymology for mintuci, explaining it as a compound of mimi (or mim) meaning 'flesh' and tumunci (トゥームーンチー) meaning 'devil'.

claims.statement: Some characterize it as a yōkai closely akin to the kappa, while others point out legends peculiar to the Ainu about the mintuci that are not seen in kappa legends.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian orang menggolongkannya sebagai yōkai yang dekat dengan kappa, sedangkan yang lain menunjukkan adanya legenda yang khas bagi Ainu tentang mintuci yang tidak terlihat pada legenda kappa.
claims.quote: Others characterize it as a yōkai, closely akin to the kappa, but others point out that there are legends peculiar to the Ainu attached to the mintuci, not seen in kappa legends.

claims.statement: Batchelor's dictionary defines mintuchi as a kind of fabulous animal said to be half human and half animal and to inhabit lakes and rivers.
claims.statement_id: Kamus Batchelor menulis mintuchi sebagai sejenis hewan fantastis yang konon setengah manusia dan setengah hewan serta menghuni danau dan sungai.
claims.quote: Mintuchi ... A kind of fabulous animal said to be half human and half animal and to inhabit lakes and rivers.

claims.statement: The dictionary entry calls these creatures "mermaids" said to have human-like bodies but hoofs instead of hands or feet, and to disembowel and devour humans they catch.
claims.statement_id: Entri kamus itu menyebut makhluk ini "putri duyung" yang konon bertubuh seperti manusia tetapi berkuku, bukan bertangan atau berkaki, dan membelah perut lalu memakan manusia yang ditangkap.
claims.quote: Mintuchi ... These mermaids are said to have bodies like those of human beings while they have hoofs instead of hands or feet. They are also said to disembowel and devour human beings when they catch them.

claims.statement: The dictionary also mentions good ones, pirika mintuci, described as fairies inhabiting the mountains and said to benefit people with their help.
claims.statement_id: Kamus itu juga menyebut ada pirika mintuci yang baik, peri yang menghuni pegunungan dan konon menguntungkan manusia dengan bantuannya.
claims.quote: There are also said to be good mermaids or pirika mintuchi, really faries inhabiting the mountains, and these are said to benefit people with their help.

claims.statement: Mishaguji names a group of kami venerated in the Suwa region.
claims.statement_id: Mishaguji adalah sebutan kelompok kami yang dihormati di wilayah Suwa.
claims.quote: Mishaguji (御左口神, 御社宮司, 御射宮司, 御社宮神; katakana: ミシャグジ), also known as Misakuji(n), Mis(h)aguchi or Mishakuji among other variants (see below), is a collective term for deities or spirits (kami) venerated in the Suwa region of Nagano Prefecture, particularly associated with the ritual practices of the Upper Shrine (Kamisha) of Suwa Taisha.

claims.statement: They were important in winter and spring shrine ceremonies.
claims.statement_id: Mereka berperan penting dalam upacara kuil pada musim dingin dan musim semi.
claims.quote: These spirits once played a key role in the shrine’s winter and spring religious ceremonies and are also enshrined in numerous smaller shrines throughout the region.

claims.statement: A ritual priest was said to summon them into people or objects.
claims.statement_id: Seorang pemimpin ritual konon memanggil mereka ke dalam manusia atau benda.
claims.quote: In these ceremonies, the Kan-no-Osa or Jinchō (神長) — also known as Jinchōkan (神長官) — a high-ranking ritual priest from the Moriya clan, would summon the Mishaguji into vessels (yorishiro), such as individuals or objects, to be temporarily inhabited during the rite.

claims.statement: The rites concluded with a formal dismissal of the spirits.
claims.statement_id: Ritual itu diakhiri dengan pelepasan roh secara resmi.
claims.quote: Upon completion, the spirits were ritually dismissed.

claims.statement: Mishaguji are believed to be spirits dwelling in rocks, trees or bamboo leaves, and in man-made objects such as stone rods (sekibō), grinding slabs (ishizara) or mortars (ishiusu).
claims.statement_id: Mishaguji dipercaya sebagai roh yang bersemayam di batu, pohon, atau daun bambu, serta benda buatan manusia seperti batang batu (sekibō), batu gerus (ishizara), atau lesung batu (ishiusu).
claims.quote: Mishaguji are believed to be spirits that dwell in rocks, trees, or bamboo leaves, as well as various man-made objects such as phallic stone rods (石棒 sekibō), grinding slabs (石皿 ishizara) or mortars (石臼 ishiusu).

claims.statement: Mishaguji are also thought to descend upon straw effigies and to possess human beings, especially during religious rituals.
claims.statement_id: Mishaguji juga dianggap turun ke boneka jerami dan merasuki manusia, terutama dalam upacara keagamaan.
claims.quote: In addition to the above, Mishaguji are also thought to descend upon straw effigies as well as possess human beings, especially during religious rituals.

claims.statement: Folk beliefs associated Mishaguji with fertility and the harvest and with healing diseases such as the common cold or pertussis.
claims.statement_id: Kepercayaan rakyat mengaitkan Mishaguji dengan kesuburan dan panen, serta sebagai penyembuh penyakit seperti pilek atau batuk rejan.
claims.quote: Folk beliefs considered Mishaguji to be associated with fertility and the harvest, as well as healers of diseases like the common cold or pertussis.

claims.statement: Mishaguji have been worshipped as tutelary deities of whole villages (ubusuna-gami) and of specific kinship groups (iwai-gami).
claims.statement_id: Mishaguji dipuja sebagai dewa pelindung seluruh desa (ubusuna-gami) maupun kelompok kekerabatan tertentu (iwai-gami).
claims.quote: Mishaguji have been worshipped as tutelary deities of whole villages (産土神 ubusuna-gami) as well as specific kinship groups (祝神 iwai-gami).

claims.statement: The name's etymology is uncertain. In the early modern period, when the Mishaguji were conflated with the divine children (mikogami) of Takeminakata, the name was explained as derived from sakuchi, 'to open up / develop the land'.
claims.statement_id: Asal nama ini tidak pasti. Pada masa awal modern, ketika Mishaguji dicampurkan dengan anak-anak ilahi (mikogami) Takeminakata, nama itu dijelaskan berasal dari istilah sakuchi, 'membuka/mengembangkan tanah'.
claims.quote: The name's etymology is uncertain. During the early modern period when the Mishaguji were conflated with the divine children (mikogami) of Takeminakata, the god of the Upper Suwa Shrine, the name was explained as being derived from the term sakuchi (闢地, lit. 'to open up / develop the land')

claims.statement: Documents produced by the Moriya in the medieval period portray the Mishaguji as lesser deities in the retinue of Suwa Myōjin (a.k.a. Takeminakata), the deity of Suwa Shrine.
claims.statement_id: Dokumen yang dibuat klan Moriya pada masa abad pertengahan menggambarkan Mishaguji sebagai dewa-dewa yang lebih rendah dalam rombongan Suwa Myōjin (alias Takeminakata), dewa Kuil Suwa.
claims.quote: Documents produced by the Moriya during the medieval period portray the Mishaguji (御左口神) as lesser deities who form the retinue of Suwa Myōjin (a.k.a. Takeminakata), the deity of Suwa Shrine.

claims.statement: By the early modern period, "Mishaguji" came to be interpreted in Suwa as an umbrella term for local kami revered as the children (mikogami) of Suwa Myōjin.
claims.statement_id: Pada masa awal modern, "Mishaguji" di Suwa dipahami sebagai istilah payung bagi kami setempat yang dihormati sebagai anak-anak Suwa Myōjin (mikogami).
claims.quote: By the early modern period, “Mishaguji” came to be interpreted in Suwa as an umbrella term for local kami who were revered as Suwa Myōjin's children (御子神, mikogami).

claims.statement: Research by a local amateur historian in the 1950s found over 750 Mishaguji shrines in Nagano Prefecture, 109 of them in the Suwa area.
claims.statement_id: Penelitian sejarawan amatir setempat pada 1950-an menemukan lebih dari 750 kuil Mishaguji di Prefektur Nagano, 109 di antaranya di kawasan Suwa.
claims.quote: Research conducted by local amateur historian Nogiku Imai in the 1950s revealed a total of over 750 '(Mi)s(h)aguji' shrines within Nagano Prefecture, 109 of which are in the Suwa area

claims.statement: Some proposed that Mishaguji were originally fertility or agricultural deities, while others viewed them as spirits inhabiting sacred natural objects such as rocks or trees.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian pengkaji mengusulkan Mishaguji semula adalah dewa kesuburan atau pertanian, sedangkan yang lain memandangnya sebagai roh yang mendiami benda alam keramat seperti batu atau pohon.
claims.quote: Some proposed that Mishaguji were originally fertility or agricultural deities, while others viewed them as spirits inhabiting sacred natural objects, such as rocks or trees.

claims.statement: Some theories hold that Mishaguji worship may trace back to the Jōmon period, since the Suwa basin was a flourishing center of Jōmon culture and many Mishaguji shrines hold Jōmon-era stone rods as sacred objects.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian teori menyatakan pemujaan Mishaguji mungkin berakar dari zaman Jōmon, karena cekungan Suwa adalah pusat budaya Jōmon yang berkembang dan banyak kuil Mishaguji memuat batang batu zaman Jōmon sebagai benda suci.
claims.quote: Some theories posit that Mishaguji worship may trace its origins to the Jōmon period, given that the Suwa basin was a flourishing center of Jōmon culture and that many Mishaguji shrines incorporate Jōmon-era phallic stone rods (石棒 sekibō) and similar prehistoric artifacts as sacred objects.

claims.statement: This origin theory has faced recent criticism, with some experts cautioning against overly speculative links between archaeological artifacts and later religious practices.
claims.statement_id: Teori asal-usul itu mendapat kritik belakangan ini; sebagian ahli mengingatkan agar tidak membuat kaitan spekulatif antara artefak arkeologi dan praktik keagamaan yang lebih kemudian.
claims.quote: However, this interpretation has faced recent criticism, with some experts cautioning against overly speculative correlations between archaeological artifacts and later religious practices.

claims.statement: It is said that about 2,000 shrines across Japan enshrine Mishaguchi, with the Maemiya of the Upper Shrine of Suwa Taisha taking the form of the head shrine.
claims.statement_id: Konon ada sekitar 2000 kuil yang memuja Mishaguchi di seluruh Jepang, dan Maemiya dari Kuil Atas Suwa Taisha berfungsi sebagai kuil induknya.
claims.quote: ミシャグチを祀る神社は全国におよそ2000社あると言われています。そしてその総本社の形をとっているのが、諏訪大社上社の前宮です。

claims.statement: Today Mishaguchi is often said to bring the blessing of prosperous descendants, but originally it is said to have been a stone deity or a snake deity.
claims.statement_id: Kini Mishaguchi sering dikatakan memberi berkah kemakmuran keturunan, tetapi pada mulanya ia disebut-sebut sebagai dewa batu atau dewa ular.
claims.quote: 現在、ミシャグチは「子孫繁栄」のご利益があるとされることが多いのですが、そもそもは「石の神」だったとも、「蛇の神」だったとも言われています。

claims.statement: The Moriya clan, as Jinchōkan priests, are said to have held all authority over Mishaguchi belief, and the secret rite of bringing the Mishaguchi kami down is held to be performable only by the Jinchōkan.
claims.statement_id: Klan Moriya, imam Jinchōkan, dikatakan memegang seluruh wewenang atas kepercayaan Mishaguchi, dan rahasia menurunkan dewa Mishaguchi dipercaya hanya dapat dilakukan oleh sang Jinchōkan.
claims.quote: そもそも、諏訪大社上社の神事を神長官守矢氏が取り仕切ってきたのも、守矢氏がミシャグチ信仰に関する一切の権限を有する司祭であり、ミシャグチ神を降ろす秘法もまた、神長官のみが行うことができるとされてきたからです。

claims.statement: Despite their longstanding presence in local tradition, the precise nature and original characteristics of the Mishaguji remain elusive, and no single definitive explanation has been established.
claims.statement_id: Meski lama hadir dalam tradisi setempat, sifat persis dan ciri asli Mishaguji tetap samar dan belum ada satu penjelasan pasti.
claims.quote: Despite their longstanding presence in local tradition, the precise nature and original characteristics of the Mishaguji remain elusive, and no single definitive explanation has been established.

claims.statement: Worship of kami with names such as 'S(h)aguji' or 'S(h)agoji' is also attested in neighboring areas and is notably widespread throughout the Kantō and Chūbu regions of Japan.
claims.statement_id: Pemujaan kami dengan nama seperti 'S(h)aguji' atau 'S(h)agoji' juga tercatat di daerah sekitar dan tersebar luas terutama di wilayah Kantō dan Chūbu di Jepang.
claims.quote: As noted above, worship of kami with names such as 'S(h)aguji' or 'S(h)agoji' are also attested in neighboring areas, being notably widespread throughout the Kantō and Chūbu regions of Japan.

claims.statement: The relation between the Ōhōri and the Jinchō is explained in mythic terms by the story of Suwa Daimyōjin establishing his presence in Suwa by subjugating the local deity Moriya (also known as Moreya), who formerly controlled the region.
claims.statement_id: Hubungan antara Ōhōri dan Jinchō dijelaskan secara mitis lewat kisah Suwa Daimyōjin yang menegakkan kehadirannya di Suwa dengan menaklukkan dewa setempat Moriya (juga disebut Moreya), yang sebelumnya menguasai wilayah itu.
claims.quote: The relation between the Ōhōri and the Jinchō is explained in mythic terms by the story of Suwa Daimyōjin establishing his presence in Suwa by subjugating the local deity Moriya (also known as Moreya), who formerly controlled the region.

claims.statement: Moreya is a Japanese deity in legends of the Suwa region.
claims.statement_id: Moreya adalah dewa Jepang dalam legenda wilayah Suwa.
claims.quote: Moreya or Moriya (洩矢神, Moriya- / Moreya-no-Kami) is a Japanese god who appears in various myths and legends of the Suwa region in Nagano Prefecture (historical Shinano Province).

claims.statement: A prominent legend describes a battle with Takeminakata.
claims.statement_id: Legenda yang terkenal menggambarkan pertempurannya dengan Takeminakata.
claims.quote: The most famous of such stories is that of his battle against Takeminakata, the god of the Grand Shrine of Suwa (Suwa Taisha).

claims.statement: The Moriya priestly family regards him as a mythical ancestor.
claims.statement_id: Keluarga pendeta Moriya menganggapnya sebagai leluhur mitologis.
claims.quote: Moriya is regarded as the mythical ancestor of the Moriya clan (守矢氏), a priestly family that formerly served in the Upper Suwa Shrine (上社, Kamisha), one of the two sub-shrines that make up Suwa Taisha.

claims.statement: He is also revered as a local protective deity near Okaya.
claims.statement_id: Ia juga dihormati sebagai dewa pelindung setempat dekat Okaya.
claims.quote: In addition, he is venerated as a local tutelary deity (ubusunagami) in a shrine in Okaya City near the Tenryū River, which in later variants of the aforementioned myth is identified as the place where Takeminakata and Moriya fought each other.

claims.statement: In one version of the legend, when the god Suwa Myōjin first manifested himself, Moriya the wicked outlaw tried to prevent the divine occupation of the land and fought with an iron ring, but the Myōjin took up a wisteria branch and subdued him.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu versi legenda, ketika dewa Suwa Myōjin pertama kali menampakkan diri, Moriya sang penjahat berusaha mencegah dewa itu menempati tanah tersebut dan bertarung dengan cincin besi, tetapi sang Myōjin mengambil ranting wisteria dan menaklukkannya.
claims.quote: In ancient times, when the venerable god (尊神, sonjin, i.e. Suwa Myōjin) first manifested himself, Moriya the wicked outlaw (洩矢ノ惡賊, Moriya no akuzoku), seeking to prevent the divine occupation of the land, took up an iron ring (鐵輪) to fight him, but the Myōjin picked up a wisteria branch and subdued [Moriya].

claims.statement: Perhaps the best-known version of the story is in the 1356 text Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba, which records it as the origin myth of Fujishima Shrine in Suwa City.
claims.statement_id: Versi cerita yang mungkin paling terkenal terdapat dalam teks tahun 1356, Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba, yang mencatatnya sebagai mitos asal-usul Kuil Fujishima di Kota Suwa.
claims.quote: What is perhaps the most well-known version of the story is found in the 1356 text Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba, where it is recorded as the origin myth of Fujishima Shrine (藤島社, Fujishima-sha) in Suwa City

claims.statement: One version has the Suwa deity or his subordinate defeating Moriya, armed with an iron ring or hook, using only a wisteria branch or vine. Another variant has Suwa Daimyōjin and/or his companion or avatar, the boy Arikazu, defeating Moriya in battle.
claims.statement_id: Satu versi mitos menyebut dewa Suwa atau bawahannya mengalahkan Moriya, yang bersenjata cincin atau kait besi, hanya dengan ranting atau sulur wisteria. Varian lain menyebut Suwa Daimyōjin dan/atau pendampingnya, anak lelaki Arikazu, mengalahkan Moriya dalam pertempuran.
claims.quote: One version of this myth involves the Suwa deity or his subordinate defeating Moriya, described as armed with an iron ring or hook, using only a wisteria (藤, fuji) branch or vine. Another variant has Suwa Daimyōjin and/or his companion or avatar, the boy Arikazu, defeating Moriya in battle.

claims.statement: Local historians have traditionally interpreted the myth as a mythologized account of a historical struggle between a powerful local polity around Lake Suwa, associated with the Moriya, and an incoming group identified with the Suwa clan.
claims.statement_id: Sejarawan setempat secara tradisional menafsirkan mitos ini sebagai catatan yang dimitoskan tentang pergulatan sejarah antara kekuatan lokal di sekitar Danau Suwa yang dikaitkan dengan Moriya dan kelompok pendatang yang diidentikkan dengan klan Suwa.
claims.quote: Whereas local historians have traditionally interpreted the myth as a mythologized account of a historical struggle between a powerful local polity in the Lake Suwa region and its environs, associated with the Moriya, and an incoming group identified with the Suwa clan

claims.statement: One view holds that the myth was gradually influenced by medieval traditions about the historical conflict between Prince Shōtoku and the anti-Buddhist Mononobe no Moriya.
claims.statement_id: Satu pandangan menyatakan mitos ini lambat laun dipengaruhi tradisi abad pertengahan tentang konflik sejarah antara Pangeran Shōtoku dan Mononobe no Moriya yang anti-Buddha.
claims.quote: One view holds that the myth was gradually influenced by medieval traditions concerning the historical conflict between Prince Shōtoku and the anti-Buddhist ōmuraji Mononobe no Moriya.

claims.statement: Another view proposes that the myth is of comparatively late origin and was built on the Shōtoku–Moriya narrative, with Mononobe no Moriya as the model for the local deity Moriya.
claims.statement_id: Pandangan lain mengusulkan mitos ini berasal dari masa yang relatif belakangan dan disusun berdasarkan kisah Shōtoku–Moriya, dengan Mononobe no Moriya menjadi model bagi dewa setempat Moriya.
claims.quote: Another proposes that the myth is of comparatively late origin and was constructed on the basis of this Shōtoku–Moriya narrative, with Mononobe no Moriya serving as the model for the local deity Moriya.

claims.statement: The deity Moriya Daijin is identified either with the Moriya of Suwa legend or the deified Mononobe no Moriya, and is considered a weather deity who causes rain to fall when angered.
claims.statement_id: Dewa Moriya Daijin diidentifikasi sebagai Moriya dalam legenda Suwa atau Mononobe no Moriya yang didewakan, dan dianggap dewa cuaca yang menurunkan hujan ketika marah.
claims.quote: The deity has been identified either with the Moriya of Suwa legend or the deified Mononobe no Moriya. ... Moriya Daijin is considered to be a weather deity who causes rain to fall when angered.

claims.statement: Local rainmaking rituals once involved provoking the god into sending rain by vandalizing the hokora (small shrine) or throwing it down the mountainside.
claims.statement_id: Ritual meminta hujan setempat dahulu dilakukan dengan memancing sang dewa agar menurunkan hujan, yaitu merusak hokora atau melemparnya ke lereng gunung.
claims.quote: Local rainmaking rituals once involved provoking the god into sending rain by vandalizing the hokora or throwing it down the mountain side.

claims.statement: One local tradition identifies Moriya as the father of the god Chikatō, an obscure deity worshiped in a handful of shrines in the Suwa basin and neighboring municipalities.
claims.statement_id: Satu tradisi setempat menyebut Moriya sebagai ayah dewa Chikatō, dewa yang kurang dikenal dan dipuja di segelintir kuil di cekungan Suwa serta kota-kota sekitarnya.
claims.quote: One local tradition identifies Moriya as the father of the god Chikatō (千鹿頭神, also 'Chikato'), an obscure deity worshiped in a handful of shrines in the Suwa basin (specifically the cities of Chino and Suwa) and the neighboring municipalities of Tatsuno and Matsumoto.

claims.statement: A story in a late source claims that Takeminakata and/or Moriya fought another local deity, Yatsukao-no-Mikoto, who died in the conflict.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah kisah dalam sumber yang belakangan menyebut Takeminakata dan/atau Moriya bertarung melawan dewa setempat lain bernama Yatsukao-no-Mikoto, yang tewas dalam konflik itu.
claims.quote: A story found in a late source claims that Takeminakata and/or Moriya (Moreya) fought another local deity named Yatsukao-no-Mikoto (矢塚男命), who died during the conflict.

claims.statement: The second-highest priestly office was Kan-no-Osa or Jinchō (later Jinchōkan), a hereditary position held by the Moriya clan, who regarded themselves as the ritual successors and heirs of the god Moriya.
claims.statement_id: Jabatan imam tertinggi kedua adalah Kan-no-Osa atau Jinchō (kemudian Jinchōkan), jabatan turun-temurun klan Moriya, yang menganggap diri mereka penerus ritual dan pewaris dewa Moriya.
claims.quote: The second-highest priestly office was that of the Kan-no-Osa or Jinchō (神長), later known as the Jinchōkan (神長官), a hereditary position held by the Moriya clan, who regarded themselves as the ritual successors and heirs of the god Moriya.

claims.statement: The Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki, for instance, states that Moriya fled into the mountain after being defeated.
claims.statement_id: Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki, misalnya, menyatakan bahwa Moriya melarikan diri ke gunung setelah dikalahkan.
claims.quote: the Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki, for instance, states that Moriya fled into the mountain after being defeated.

claims.statement: A number of other texts refer to the god as Moriya Daijin, an epithet more often used for the historical Mononobe no Moriya in medieval and later sources.
claims.statement_id: Sejumlah teks lain menyebut dewa ini Moriya Daijin, julukan yang lebih sering dipakai untuk tokoh sejarah Mononobe no Moriya dalam sumber abad pertengahan dan sesudahnya.
claims.quote: A number of other texts (see below) meanwhile refer to the god as Moriya Daijin (守屋大臣), an epithet more often used for the historical Mononobe no Moriya in medieval and later sources.

claims.statement: The officeholder also had the prerogative of summoning and installing the Mishaguji (divine spirits associated with certain Upper Shrine rites) in objects serving as their vessels (yorishiro), and of dismissing them when the rites ended.
claims.statement_id: Pemegang jabatan itu juga berhak memanggil dan menempatkan Mishaguji (roh ilahi yang terkait dengan upacara tertentu Kuil Atas) ke dalam benda wadahnya (yorishiro), dan melepasnya ketika upacara selesai.
claims.quote: He also had the prerogative of summoning and installing the Mishaguji (divine spirits associated with certain Upper Shrine rites) in objects that served as their vessels (yorishiro), and of dismissing them when the rites were concluded.

claims.statement: Behind the Upper Shrine, straddling the border between the cities of Suwa and Ina, stands the 1,650-metre-high Mount Moriya.
claims.statement_id: Di belakang Kuil Atas, membentang di perbatasan kota Suwa dan Ina, berdiri Gunung Moriya setinggi 1.650 meter.
claims.quote: Behind the Upper Shrine, straddling the border between the cities of Suwa and Ina, stands the 1,650 metre-high Mount Moriya.

claims.statement: A magazine article names Moriya-gami, the ancestral deity of the Moriya family, as the deity in Suwa myth thought to hold the key.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah artikel majalah menyebut dewa dalam mitos Suwa yang dianggap memegang kuncinya adalah dewa leluhur keluarga Moriya, Moriya-gami.
claims.quote: 諏訪に伝わる神話の中には、そのキーを握ると思われる神の話があります。その神こそ、守矢家の祖先神「洩矢神(モリヤガミ)」です。

claims.statement: Quoted from the Suwa Daimyōjin Engi Ekotoba (1356): when the evil deity Moriya tried to hinder the deity's dwelling, Moriya fought with an iron ring, and the Myōjin took a wisteria branch and subdued him.
claims.statement_id: Kutipan dari Suwa Daimyōjin Engi Ekotoba (1356): ketika dewa jahat Moriya berusaha menghalangi kediaman sang dewa, Moriya bertarung dengan cincin besi, dan sang Myōjin mengambil ranting wisteria dan menaklukkannya.
claims.quote: 洩矢の悪神神居を妨げんとせし時、洩矢は鉄輪を持して争い、明神は藤の枝をとりてこれを伏し給う。ついに邪輪を降し正法を興す(「諏訪大明神縁起絵詞」1356年より)

claims.statement: Nozuchi is a Japanese yōkai sometimes interpreted as a field spirit.
claims.statement_id: Nozuchi adalah yōkai Jepang yang kadang ditafsirkan sebagai roh padang.
claims.quote: 野槌（のづち）は、日本に伝わる妖怪。野つ霊、野椎とも。野の精霊（「野つ霊（ち）」の意）であるとも言われる。

claims.statement: Its thick, serpentine body is compared with a mallet without a handle.
claims.statement_id: Tubuhnya yang tebal dan mirip ular disamakan dengan palu tanpa gagang.
claims.quote: 外見は蛇のようだが、胴は太く、頭部に口がある以外は目も鼻もなく、ちょうど柄のない槌（つち）のような形をしている。

claims.statement: Accounts give it a mouth but no eyes or nose.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah memberinya mulut, tetapi tanpa mata atau hidung.
claims.quote: 外見は蛇のようだが、胴は太く、頭部に口がある以外は目も鼻もなく、ちょうど柄のない槌（つち）のような形をしている。

claims.statement: It is said to roll down slopes and slowly climb back.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon berguling menuruni lereng lalu merayap naik kembali.
claims.quote: They are slow movers, and get about by rolling and tumbling down slopes, then slowly inching their way back up.

claims.statement: A description gives it bristly hair resembling a caterpillar’s covering.
claims.statement_id: Satu gambaran memberinya rambut kasar seperti penutup tubuh ulat.
claims.quote: Their bodies are covered in a bristly fur, much like a hairy caterpillar.

claims.statement: One regional account in Nara describes it eating deer.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah daerah di Nara menggambarkannya memakan rusa.
claims.quote: In Nara, they are known to feed on deer.

issues.message: Pernyataan hampir tidak berbagi kata dengan kutipannya sendiri. Pastikan kutipan ini benar-benar mendukung pernyataan ini (bukan kutipan milik klaim lain).

claims.statement: Nuribotoke is a yōkai pictured in Japanese supernatural scrolls.
claims.statement_id: Nuribotoke adalah yōkai yang digambar dalam gulungan makhluk gaib Jepang.
claims.quote: The Nuribotoke (塗仏) is a yōkai found in Japanese yōkai emaki such as the Hyakkai Zukan by Sawaki Suushi.

claims.statement: Toriyama Sekien also depicted it in an illustrated collection.
claims.statement_id: Toriyama Sekien juga menggambarnya dalam kumpulan ilustrasi.
claims.quote: They are also depicted in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien.

claims.statement: Its image resembles a dark-skinned animated corpse.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya menyerupai mayat hidup berkulit gelap.
claims.quote: They are depicted as an animated corpse with darkened skin and dangling eyeballs.

claims.statement: The eyes are shown hanging from their sockets.
claims.statement_id: Matanya ditampilkan menjuntai dari rongga mata.
claims.quote: They are depicted as an animated corpse with darkened skin and dangling eyeballs.

claims.statement: A later account gives it deceptive predictions.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan menyebut ia memberikan ramalan menipu.
claims.quote: Occasionally they try to trick foolish humans by giving false prophecies.

claims.statement: That account says it returns to the household altar before dawn.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menyebut ia kembali ke altar rumah sebelum fajar.
claims.quote: Nuribotoke must return to the butsudan before sunrise, and they vanish altogether during the day.

claims.statement: Oboroguruma is a cart yōkai in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Oboroguruma adalah yōkai kereta dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Oboroguruma (朧車, hazy cart) is a Yōkai in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: Its form is a ghostly ox cart with a face.
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya kereta lembu gaib yang memiliki wajah.
claims.quote: The Oboroguruma is a ghostly ox cart with a face on it.

claims.statement: A legend places its creaking sounds on misty moonlit nights in Kyoto.
claims.statement_id: Satu legenda menempatkan bunyi deritnya pada malam berkabut dan diterangi bulan di Kyoto.
claims.quote: Legend has it that on misty nights that are lit by the moon in Kyoto, people can hear squeaking sounds coming from an ox cart.

claims.statement: The cart is said to wait outside a person’s house.
claims.statement_id: Kereta itu konon berada di luar rumah seseorang.
claims.quote: When the person steps outside, they would find the Oboroguruma parked outside their home.

claims.statement: Toriyama Sekien included the figure with a description in his illustrated books.
claims.statement_id: Toriyama Sekien memuat sosok itu beserta keterangan dalam buku bergambarnya.
claims.quote: When Toriyama Sekien published his yōkai bestiaries, he included the oboroguruma and gave a description.

claims.statement: One interpretation links it with the carriage rivalry in The Tale of Genji.
claims.statement_id: Satu tafsir menghubungkannya dengan persaingan kereta dalam The Tale of Genji.
claims.quote: He linked it to a famous scene in The Tale of Genji when Lady Rokujō and her rival Lady Aoi competed for a parking space and got into a carriage fight.

claims.statement: Oshira-sama is a household protective deity in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Oshira-sama adalah dewa pelindung rumah dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Oshirasama (Japanese: おしら様, おしらさま, お白様, オシラ様, or オシラサマ, Hepburn: oshira-sama) is a tutelary deity of the home in Japanese folklore.

claims.statement: Some household customs restrict meat and who may touch its sacred image.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian kebiasaan rumah membatasi daging dan siapa yang boleh menyentuh wujud sucinya.
claims.quote: It is believed that when Oshirasama is in a person's home, one cannot eat meat and only women are allowed to touch it.

claims.statement: Its images combine the faces of a horse and a maiden.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya memadukan wajah kuda dan perempuan muda.
claims.quote: Born from a stallion and human woman, "images of this god [Oshira] are usually composed of the faces of a horse and a maiden." The festival day for Oshirasama is called meinichi (命日, or a death anniversary).

claims.statement: One myth connects the deity with love between a woman and a stallion.
claims.statement_id: Satu mitos menghubungkan dewa itu dengan cinta antara perempuan dan kuda jantan.
claims.quote: According to myth, Oshira-sama was born from a stallion and a maiden falling in love.

claims.statement: In the myth, the maiden's angry father killed the stallion and stripped its skin; the skin wrapped around the daughter and took her to heaven. Later they descended as silkworms and became guardian gods of families called Jūrokuzen no kami.
claims.statement_id: Dalam mitos, ayah sang gadis yang murka membunuh kuda jantan dan menguliti kulitnya; kulit itu membungkus sang putri dan membawanya ke langit. Keduanya kemudian turun sebagai ulat sutra, lalu menjadi dewa penjaga keluarga yang disebut Jūrokuzen no kami.
claims.quote: Angered by the affair, the maiden's father killed the stallion and stripped it of its skin. "The skin then wrapped itself around the daughter and took her up to heaven. Later, they descended from heaven, incarnated as silkworms. After this they became the guardian gods of families and were called Jūrokuzen no kami."

claims.statement: The original story can be read in Sōushén Jì, a Chinese classic written in the fourth century.
claims.statement_id: Kisah asli mitos ini dapat dibaca dalam Sōushén Jì, karya klasik Tiongkok yang ditulis pada abad keempat.
claims.quote: The original story can be read in Sōushén Jì, a Chinese classic written in the fourth century

claims.statement: Having emerged from great hardship, the Oshira god is often invoked by itako or shamans to provide healing to individuals facing similar turmoil in their personal lives.
claims.statement_id: Karena lahir dari kesulitan besar, dewa Oshira sering dipanggil oleh itako atau dukun untuk menyembuhkan orang yang menghadapi gejolak serupa dalam hidup pribadinya.
claims.quote: Having emerged from great hardship, the Oshira god is often invoked by Itakos or shamans to provide healing to individuals facing similar turmoil in their personal lives.

claims.statement: The deity is also a character in the film Spirited Away; in the American version of the film the character is called Radish Spirit.
claims.statement_id: Dewa ini juga menjadi tokoh dalam film Spirited Away; dalam versi Amerika film itu tokoh tersebut disebut Radish Spirit.
claims.quote: The deity is also a character for the film Spirited Away. In the American version of the film the character is called Radish Spirit.

claims.statement: Oshirasama is a tutelary of the home (ie no kami) found throughout Japan's northeastern region, also called Oshirabotoke ("the Oshira Buddha").
claims.statement_id: Oshirasama adalah dewa pelindung rumah (ie no kami) yang ditemukan di seluruh wilayah timur laut Jepang, juga disebut Oshirabotoke ("Buddha Oshira").
claims.quote: A tutelary of the home (ie no kami) found throughout Japan's northeastern region; also referred to as Oshirabotoke ("the Oshira Buddha").

claims.statement: Oshirasama is commonly viewed as a tutelary of agriculture and silkworm production, but little agreement has been reached on the etymology of the name Oshira and the kami's specific characteristics.
claims.statement_id: Oshirasama umumnya dipandang sebagai dewa pelindung pertanian dan produksi ulat sutra, tetapi belum ada kesepakatan tentang asal nama Oshira dan ciri khusus kami ini.
claims.quote: Although Oshirasama is commonly viewed as a tutelary of agriculture and silkworm production, little agreement has been reached regarding the etymology of the name Oshira and the kami's specific characteristics.

claims.statement: The object of Oshirasama worship generally consists of a pair of mulberry sticks (occasionally bamboo) about 30 cm long, with male and female faces (or a horse's head) carved or painted in ink on one end.
claims.statement_id: Benda pemujaan Oshirasama umumnya berupa sepasang tongkat murbei (kadang bambu) sepanjang sekitar 30 cm dengan wajah laki-laki dan perempuan (atau kepala kuda) yang diukir atau dilukis dengan tinta di salah satu ujungnya.
claims.quote: The object of Oshirasama worship generally consists of a pair of sticks of mulberry (ocassionally bamboo) about 30 cm long, with male and female faces (or a horse's head) carved or painted in ink on one end.

claims.statement: The images are clothed in layers of cloth called osendaku, which are added to each year.
claims.statement_id: Gambar-gambar itu dikenakan lapisan kain bernama osendaku yang ditambah setiap tahun.
claims.quote: The images are clothed in layers of cloth called osendaku which are added to each year.

claims.statement: Devotees of Oshirasama may be individual homes, lineage groups, geographically linked community groups and confraternities (kō), but all are characterized by women playing the central roles in the cult.
claims.statement_id: Penganut Oshirasama dapat berupa rumah tangga, kelompok garis keturunan, kelompok komunitas setempat, dan perkumpulan (kō), tetapi semuanya ditandai oleh peran sentral perempuan dalam pemujaan itu.
claims.quote: Devotees of Oshirasama may be composed of individual homes, lineage groups (dōzokudan), geographically linked community groups, and confraternities (kō), but all are characterized by the fact that women play the central roles in the cult.

claims.statement: The festival day of Oshirasama, called meinichi, falls on the sixteenth day of the first, third and ninth months of the lunar calendar.
claims.statement_id: Hari raya Oshirasama, yang disebut meinichi, jatuh pada hari keenam belas bulan pertama, ketiga, dan kesembilan menurut kalender lunar.
claims.quote: Called meinichi, the festival day to Oshirasama falls on the sixteenth day of the first, third and ninth months according to the lunar calender.

claims.statement: The itako faces the Oshirasama on an altar and reads a mantra to invoke the kami's presence, then holds one Oshirasama in each hand and moves the dolls as if dancing while intoning the mantra, a rite called oshira asobase.
claims.statement_id: Itako menghadap Oshirasama di altar dan membaca mantra untuk memanggil kehadiran kami, lalu memegang satu Oshirasama di tiap tangan dan menggerakkannya seperti menari sambil melafalkan mantra, ritus bernama oshira asobase.
claims.quote: The itako faces the Oshirasama enshrined on an altar, and reads a mantra meant to invoke the presence of the kami. Next, the itako holds one Oshirasama in each hand and while intoning the Oshira mantra, moves the dolls as though they were dancing, a rite called oshira asobase.

claims.statement: Finally, the itako performs divinations for the village or individual households.
claims.statement_id: Pada akhirnya itako melakukan ramalan untuk desa atau rumah tangga perorangan.
claims.quote: Finally, the itako performs divinations for the village or individual households.

claims.statement: The Oshirasama cult involves taboos: Oshirasama is said to disdain eggs and chickens and the meat of two- and four-legged animals, and breaking a taboo may result in a twisted mouth or major illness.
claims.statement_id: Pemujaan Oshirasama mengandung pantangan: dikatakan Oshirasama tidak menyukai telur dan ayam serta daging hewan berkaki dua dan empat. Melanggar pantangan dapat berakibat mulut mencong atau sakit berat.
claims.quote: The Oshirasama cult involves taboos, as it is said that Oshirasama disdains eggs and chickens, as well as the meat of two- and four-legged animals. Breaking one of the taboos may result in a twisted mouth or major illness.

claims.statement: If one fails to worship Oshirasama properly, Oshirasama may visit the family with a curse, or fly away and mysteriously disappear.
claims.statement_id: Bila seseorang tidak memuja Oshirasama dengan semestinya, Oshirasama dapat menimpakan kutukan pada keluarga itu, atau terbang pergi dan menghilang secara misterius.
claims.quote: In addition, should one fail to worship Oshirasama properly, the Oshirasama may visit the family with a curse, or fly away and mysteriously disappear.

claims.statement: Otoroshi is a yōkai shown in Japanese scrolls and illustrated books.
claims.statement_id: Otoroshi adalah yōkai yang ditampilkan dalam gulungan dan buku bergambar Jepang.
claims.quote: Otoroshi (おとろし; "scary") are a Japanese yōkai that appear in several yōkai emaki, such as the Hyakkai Zukan by Sawaki Suushi and the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien (1776).

claims.statement: Several alternate names are associated with the figure.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa nama lain dikaitkan dengan sosok itu.
claims.quote: Other names include Odoro-odoro, Ke Ippai (毛一杯, "much hair"), Odoroshi, Odoro-odoroshi, and Otoron.

claims.statement: One explanation relates its name to a word for frightening.
claims.statement_id: Satu penjelasan menghubungkan namanya dengan kata yang berarti menakutkan.
claims.quote: The Otoroshi's name likely comes from a regional corruption of the word osoroshii meaning scary, frightening or disheveled.

claims.statement: Another proposed origin links the name with heavily grown hair.
claims.statement_id: Usulan asal nama lainnya menghubungkannya dengan rambut yang sangat lebat.
claims.quote: The yōkai researchers Tada and Kenji Murakami posit that the word "odorogami" (棘髪), meaning extremely long growths of hair, is another origin for the names.

claims.statement: A later account gives it a hairy body with claws and tusks.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan memberinya tubuh berbulu dengan cakar dan taring.
claims.quote: Otoroshi appear as hairy, hunched, four-legged beasts with fierce claws and tusks.

claims.statement: That account portrays it as a guardian of sacred places.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menggambarkannya sebagai penjaga tempat suci.
claims.quote: Interactions : Otoroshi act as a kind of guardian of these holy places.

claims.statement: Sankai is a birth monster in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Sankai adalah monster kelahiran dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: In Japanese mythology, a sankai (産怪, sankai; literally, "birth monster") is a yōkai (praeternatural creature) that is born to a woman.

claims.statement: The myth connects its birth with insufficient care during pregnancy.
claims.statement_id: Mitos menghubungkan kelahirannya dengan kurangnya perawatan selama kehamilan.
claims.quote: According to myth, when due care is not given during pregnancy, a sankai would emerge instead.

claims.statement: An Okayama version is called oketsu.
claims.statement_id: Versi dari Okayama disebut oketsu.
claims.quote: The story of the oketsu (オケツ) comes from Okayama Prefecture.

claims.statement: That version resembles a turtle with hair on its back.
claims.statement_id: Versi itu menyerupai kura-kura dengan rambut di punggung.
claims.quote: From outer appearance, it looks similar to a turtle, and it has hair growing on its back.

claims.statement: It is said to crawl beneath the house immediately after birth.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon merangkak ke bawah rumah segera setelah lahir.
claims.quote: As soon as it is born, it starts to crawl on the floor and attempts to escape underneath the house.

claims.statement: Other regions use names such as kekkai and kekke.
claims.statement_id: Wilayah lain memakai nama seperti kekkai dan kekke.
claims.quote: The sankai is known as a kekkai (血塊, ケッカイ) in Saitama Prefecture and Kanagawa Prefecture, and kekke (ケッケ) in Nagano Prefecture.

claims.statement: In the oketsu story from Okayama Prefecture, if it is not captured and killed right away it is said to crawl underneath the sleeping mother and kill her.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah oketsu dari Prefektur Okayama, bila tidak segera ditangkap dan dibunuh, makhluk itu konon merangkak ke bawah ibu yang sedang tidur dan membunuhnya.
claims.quote: The story of the oketsu (オケツ) comes from Okayama Prefecture. ... If not captured and killed right away, it is said to crawl underneath the sleeping mother and kill her.

claims.statement: Legends about the kekkai's appearance are sparse, but it is said to look like cattle and to be hairy; it is also said to bury under the house to kill its mother.
claims.statement_id: Legenda tentang wujud kekkai jarang, tetapi konon ia menyerupai sapi dan berbulu; ia juga konon menggali masuk ke bawah rumah untuk membunuh ibunya.
claims.quote: Legends about its outer appearance are sparse, however it is said to look like cattle and is said to be hairy. Kekkai is also said to bury under the house to kill its mother.

claims.statement: In Urawa, a practice existed of surrounding the bottom of the house with byōbu (folding screens) during childbirth to prevent this maneuver.
claims.statement_id: Di Urawa pernah ada kebiasaan mengelilingi bagian bawah rumah dengan byōbu (sekat lipat) saat persalinan untuk mencegah gerakan itu.
claims.quote: In Urawa, a practice existed of surrounding the bottom of a house with byōbu during childbirth to prevent this maneuver.

claims.statement: In the Ashigara region of Kanagawa Prefecture the sankai is said to move at once while still bloody; if the kekkai escaped, the woman was believed to die, so someone had to guard the irori (hearth), typically equipped with a shamoji.
claims.statement_id: Di wilayah Ashigara, Prefektur Kanagawa, sankai konon bergerak segera selagi masih berlumuran darah; bila kekkai berhasil kabur, sang perempuan dipercaya meninggal, sehingga seseorang harus menjaga irori (perapian), biasanya dengan memegang shamoji.
claims.quote: In the Ashigara region of Kanagawa Prefecture, the sankai is said to move immediately while still bloody, the jizaikagi of an irori, or hearth. If the kekkai successfully escapes, the woman was believed to die. In order to prevent this, someone would have to guard the irori, typically equipped with a shamoji.

claims.statement: It is theorized that the name kekkai may derive from kekkai (結界), meaning an area restricted for religious reasons.
claims.statement_id: Ada teori bahwa nama kekkai mungkin berasal dari kekkai (結界), yakni kawasan yang dibatasi karena alasan keagamaan.
claims.quote: It is theorized that the etymology may derive from kekkai (結界), meaning an area restricted for religious reasons.

claims.statement: Folklorist Iwao Hino recalls seeing a kekkai at a freak show as a child; the show said a woman gave birth to it at a university hospital, but Hino later believed it must have been a trained night monkey.
claims.statement_id: Folklorawan Iwao Hino mengingat pernah melihat kekkai di pertunjukan keanehan semasa kecil; pertunjukan itu menyebutnya dilahirkan seorang perempuan di rumah sakit universitas, tetapi Hino kemudian meyakini itu monyet malam yang dijinakkan.
claims.quote: Folklorist Iwao Hino recalls spotting a kekkai at a freak show during childhood. The show stated that it was given birth by a woman at a University hospital, however Hino later believed that it must have been a trained night monkey.

claims.statement: It is said that fetuses lost to miscarriage, and deformed or premature infants born from abnormal births such as premature birth, were formerly regarded as yōkai of this kind.
claims.statement_id: Dikatakan bahwa janin hasil keguguran serta bayi cacat atau prematur dari kelahiran tidak normal seperti kelahiran dini dahulu dipandang sebagai yōkai semacam ini.
claims.quote: そのために流産で産まれた胎児、早産などの異常出産で産まれた奇形児や未熟児が、これらのように妖怪視されたといわれる。

claims.statement: The kekkai, a yōkai of Saitama and Kanagawa Prefectures (called kekke in Nagano), is said to have two tongues and hair growing backwards, or a mouth and nose like a cow and a shaggy body.
claims.statement_id: Kekkai, yōkai dari Prefektur Saitama dan Kanagawa (di Nagano disebut kekke), konon berlidah dua dengan bulu tumbuh terbalik, atau bermulut dan berhidung seperti sapi serta berbulu lebat.
claims.quote: 血塊(けっかい)は、埼玉県、神奈川県に伝わる妖怪。長野県ではケッケという。舌が二枚有り毛が逆さに生えている、または口や鼻が牛に似て毛むくじゃらの姿をしているといわれる。

claims.statement: The Digital Daijisen dictionary by Shōgakukan glosses "kekkai" as a popular name for the loris, a kind of monkey, which was exhibited as a spectacle in the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Kamus Digital Daijisen terbitan Shōgakukan menjelaskan "kekkai" sebagai nama populer untuk sejenis monyet, yaitu loris, yang pada zaman Edo dipertontonkan.
claims.quote: 小学館のデジタル大辞泉は「けっかい」について「猿の一種、ロリスの俗称。江戸時代、見世物にされた。」としている。

claims.statement: Shibaemon-tanuki is a supernatural tanuki from Awaji Island.
claims.statement_id: Shibaemon-tanuki adalah tanuki gaib dari Pulau Awaji.
claims.quote: Shibaemon-tanuki, or Shibaemon-danuki (芝右衛門狸 or 柴右衛門狸) is a bake-danuki told in the legends of Awaji island, Hyōgo Prefecture.

claims.statement: He is counted among Japan’s three famous tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Ia dihitung sebagai salah satu dari tiga tanuki terkenal Jepang.
claims.quote: Along with Danzaburou-danuki of Sado island and the Yashima no Hage-tanuki of Kagawa Prefecture, he is counted among the "three famous tanuki of Japan." He is also written about in the colorful stories collection of the Edo period, the Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.

claims.statement: An Edo-period illustrated tale collection records him.
claims.statement_id: Kumpulan cerita bergambar zaman Edo mencatat sosoknya.
claims.quote: Along with Danzaburou-danuki of Sado island and the Yashima no Hage-tanuki of Kagawa Prefecture, he is counted among the "three famous tanuki of Japan." He is also written about in the colorful stories collection of the Edo period, the Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.

claims.statement: A tale describes a dog killing him while he is disguised as a human.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita menggambarkan anjing membunuhnya ketika ia menyamar sebagai manusia.
claims.quote: While disguised as a human and in the middle of performing an act, he was attacked by a dog and killed, but the details of the tale differ depending on region and literature.

claims.statement: One account names his wife Omasu.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menyebut istrinya bernama Omasu.
claims.quote: Mikuma (三熊山) behind the city of Sumoto, Awaji island, he lived with his wife Omasu (お増) and on moonlight nights with good weather, he drummed his belly.

claims.statement: His stories combine deceptive tricks with help for lost travelers.
claims.statement_id: Cerita-ceritanya memadukan tipuan dengan bantuan bagi pelancong yang tersesat.
claims.quote: He performed mischief such as disguising himself as a human and making tree leaves seem like gold and sell them, but at the same time he did kind deeds such as guiding along humans who stumbled into the mountain while drunk, so nobody hated him.

claims.statement: Shibaemon-tanuki lived at the summit of Mt. Mikuma behind the city of Sumoto on Awaji island with his wife Omasu, and on fine moonlit nights he drummed his belly.
claims.statement_id: Shibaemon-tanuki tinggal di puncak Gunung Mikuma di belakang Kota Sumoto, Pulau Awaji, bersama istrinya Omasu, dan pada malam berbulan yang cerah ia menabuh perutnya.
claims.quote: While Shibaemon-tanuki was at the summit of Mt. Mikuma (三熊山) behind the city of Sumoto, Awaji island, he lived with his wife Omasu (お増) and on moonlight nights with good weather, he drummed his belly.

claims.statement: The people he had been kind to made offerings of one-shō bottles of sake at the place where he dwelled.
claims.statement_id: Orang-orang yang pernah ditolongnya mempersembahkan botol sake satu sho ke tempat tinggalnya.
claims.quote: The people he has been kind to made offerings of 1 sho bottles of sake to where he dwelled.

claims.statement: One time Shibaemon heard of a very popular play called Nakaza being performed in Naniwa (now Osaka city), and he and Omasu disguised themselves as humans and went to Osaka.
claims.statement_id: Suatu kali Shibaemon mendengar ada pertunjukan sangat populer bernama Nakaza di Naniwa (kini Kota Osaka), lalu ia dan Omasu menyamar sebagai manusia pergi ke Osaka.
claims.quote: One time, Shibaemon heard that there was a very popular play called Nakaza that was being performed in Naniwa (now Osaka city) and disguised himself and Omasu both as humans to Osaka.

claims.statement: Stricken with grief, Shibaemon was about to return to Awaji but decided to watch the play Omasu had wanted to see, and used a technique to change tree leaves into gold to go to the theater.
claims.statement_id: Shibaemon yang berduka hendak kembali ke Awaji, tetapi memutuskan menonton pertunjukan yang diinginkan Omasu dan memakai teknik mengubah daun pohon menjadi emas lalu pergi ke teater.
claims.quote: Shibaemon, who was stricken with grief, was about to return to Awaji, but decided to at least watch the play that Omasu wanted to see and used a technique to change tree leaves into gold and went to the theater.

claims.statement: At the theater, tree leaves were found mixed in with the admission fees, so people suspected a bake-danuki had slipped in among the guests and a guard dog was put on alert.
claims.statement_id: Namun di teater ditemukan daun pohon bercampur dalam uang karcis, sehingga orang curiga ada bake-danuki menyelinap di antara penonton dan seekor anjing penjaga disiagakan.
claims.quote: However, at the theater, there were tree leaves that were mixed in with the admission fees, so they suspected that a bake-danuki has slipped in among the guests and a guard dog was put on alert.

claims.statement: Shibaemon hid his fear and passed through the entrance, but when his confidence slipped the dog rushed to attack; he immediately returned to his tanuki form, was chased by the people with the dog and finally hit on the head and killed.
claims.statement_id: Shibaemon menyembunyikan rasa takutnya dan melewati pintu masuk, tetapi saat kepercayaan dirinya lengah, anjing itu menerjang; ia segera kembali ke wujud tanuki, dikejar orang-orang yang membawa anjing, dan akhirnya dipukul di kepala hingga tewas.
claims.quote: Shibaemon hid his fear and passed through the entrance, but within a gap of his confidence, the dog rushed to attack. Shibaemon immediately returned to his appearance as a tanuki, was chased around by the people who brought the dog and finally hit in the head and killed.

claims.statement: After Shibaemon's death, audiences at Nakaza fell and a rumor spread that it was a curse for having killed him; when the theater deified Shibaemon, the number of guests returned.
claims.statement_id: Setelah Shibaemon mati, penonton Nakaza berkurang dan beredar kabar bahwa itu kutukan karena membunuhnya; ketika teater itu mendewakan Shibaemon, jumlah penonton kembali.
claims.quote: After Shibaemon's death, the people who came to see Nakaza decreased and there was a rumor that "it was a curse from having killed Shibaemon," so when the theater deified Shibaemon, the number of guests returned.

claims.statement: Afterwards Shibaemon, as a popular god, was deeply worshipped by many actors such as Nakamura Ganjirou, Kataoka Nizaemon and Fujiyama Kanbi.
claims.statement_id: Kemudian Shibaemon, sebagai dewa yang populer, dipuja dengan sungguh-sungguh oleh banyak aktor seperti Nakamura Ganjirou, Kataoka Nizaemon, dan Fujiyama Kanbi.
claims.quote: Afterwards, Shibaemon, as a popular god, was deeply worshipped by many actors such as Nakamura Ganjirou, Kataoka Nizaemon and Fujiyama Kanbi.

claims.statement: The Shrine of Shibaemon now stands near the castle ruins of Sumoto at the peak of Mt. Mikuma, and because of the legend of Shibaemon, who liked theater, many performers still visit it.
claims.statement_id: Kini kuil Shibaemon berada di dekat reruntuhan kastil Sumoto di puncak Gunung Mikuma, dan karena legenda Shibaemon yang menyukai teater, banyak pemain pertunjukan masih mengunjungi kuil itu.
claims.quote: Now, the Shrine of Shibaemon is near the castle ruins of Sumoto at the peak of Mt. Mikuma and due to the legend of Shibaemon, who liked theater, there are many performers who visit the shrine even now.

claims.statement: The Shibaemon Daimyoujin deified in Nakaza also had a "return home" in the year 2000 and is now deified in the Sumoto Hachiman-jinja.
claims.statement_id: Shibaemon Daimyoujin yang didewakan di Nakaza juga "pulang kampung" pada tahun 2000 dan kini dipuja di Sumoto Hachiman-jinja.
claims.quote: The Shibaemon Daimyoujin (柴右衛門大明神) that was deified in Nakaza also had a "return home" in the year 2000 and is now deified in the Sumoto Hachiman-jinja.

claims.statement: In one legend, the next morning the soldier turned into a bloodstained tanuki, and it was Shibaemon-tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu legenda, keesokan paginya wujud prajurit itu berubah menjadi tanuki berlumuran darah, dan itu adalah Shibaemon-tanuki.
claims.quote: The next morning, when the government officials visited to inspect again, the soldier's appearance turned into a bloodstained tanuki. It was Shibaemon-tanuki.

claims.statement: In one version, there was once a peasant called Shibaemon on Awaji, and an old tanuki came to ask for food scraps; feeling pity, he deliberately left some food for the tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu versi, di Awaji dahulu ada seorang petani bernama Shibaemon, dan seekor tanuki tua datang meminta sisa makanan; karena kasihan, ia sengaja menyisakan makanan untuknya.
claims.quote: In the past, in Awaji, there was a peasant called Shibaemon, and an old tanuki came to him and requested for food scraps, and feeling pity, he expressly left some food for the tanuki.

claims.statement: There are theories that the reality behind the legend of Shibaemon-tanuki was an excuse for the Kougo Jihen, a struggle that broke out between Sumoto and Awa.
claims.statement_id: Ada teori bahwa kenyataan di balik legenda Shibaemon-tanuki adalah dalih bagi Kougo Jihen, pergolakan antara Sumoto dan Awa.
claims.quote: There are theories that reality of the legend of Shibaemon-tanuki is that it was an excuse for the Kougo Jihen, a struggle that broke out between Sumoto and Awa

claims.statement: In the Edo period, at the base of Mount Seimi in Awa Province (now Tokushima prefecture), there was a theater business at the grounds of Kan'on-ji that earned great popularity.
claims.statement_id: Pada zaman Edo, di kaki Gunung Seimi di Provinsi Awa (kini Prefektur Tokushima), ada usaha teater di halaman Kuil Kan'on-ji yang sangat populer.
claims.quote: In the Edo period, at the base of Mount Seimi (勢見山) in Awa Province (now Tokushima prefecture), there was a theater business at the grounds of Kan'on-ji, and it earned great popularity.

claims.statement: Tanuki statues around Sumoto are inspired by Shibaemon, a tanuki in a folk tale passed down in Sumoto for generations.
claims.statement_id: Patung-patung tanuki di berbagai tempat di Sumoto terinspirasi dari Shibaemon, tanuki dalam cerita rakyat yang diwariskan turun-temurun di Sumoto.
claims.quote: As you walk around Sumoto, you will come across charming tanuki statues in various places. These statues are inspired by Shibaemon, a tanuki who appears in a folk tale that has been passed down in Sumoto for generations.

claims.statement: The "Sumoto Eight Tanuki Story" is a sightseeing route with eight tanuki statues based on the legends of Shibaemon; each statue has its own name, blessing and story.
claims.statement_id: "Sumoto Eight Tanuki Story" adalah rute wisata dengan delapan patung tanuki berdasarkan legenda Shibaemon; tiap patung punya nama, berkat, dan kisahnya sendiri.
claims.quote: The "Sumoto Eight Tanuki Story" is a sightseeing route featuring eight tanuki statues based on the legends of Shibaemon. Eight statues modeled on Shibaemon and his companions are located at various spots around the city. Each has its own name, blessing, and story.

claims.statement: Shōkera is a Japanese yōkai pictured in Edo-period scrolls.
claims.statement_id: Shōkera adalah yōkai Jepang yang digambar dalam gulungan zaman Edo.
claims.quote: The Shōkera (しょうけら; lit. Mole Cricket Spirit) is a Japanese yōkai found in Edo Period yōkai emaki such as, the Hyakkai Zukan and the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō.

claims.statement: Several spellings are recorded for its name.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa ejaan dicatat untuk namanya.
claims.quote: They can also be written しゃうけら, せうけら, as well as 精螻蛄.

claims.statement: The old illustrations lack explanatory text, leaving its nature uncertain.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi lama tidak memiliki keterangan, sehingga sifatnya tidak pasti.
claims.quote: In the Hyakkai Zukan, Gazu Hyakki Yagyō etc., they appear only in pictures with no explanatory text, so what kind of yōkai they are is a matter of speculation.

claims.statement: Sekien depicts it peering through a roof skylight.
claims.statement_id: Sekien menggambarnya mengintip melalui jendela atap.
claims.quote: The Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien depicts a shōkera looking in through the skylight of a house's roof.

claims.statement: Later literature interprets this as watching whether people observe Kōshin rules.
claims.statement_id: Karya belakangan menafsirkannya sebagai pengawasan terhadap kepatuhan pada aturan Kōshin.
claims.quote: Yōkai-related literature starting in Shōwa and Heisei began to give the interpretation that this is surveillance to see whether people are following the rules of Kōshin-Machi day, and it is supposed that the shōkera would give a punishment by three fingers with sharp nails on those who break the rule.

claims.statement: In folk religion there is a custom called "shōkera" in the Kōshin-Machi, based on a belief in an insect called the Three Corpses inside the body that on Kōshin night rises to the skies and reports the person's crimes to the Ten-Tei (heavenly god), who then takes that person's life.
claims.statement_id: Dalam agama rakyat ada kebiasaan bernama "shōkera" pada Kōshin-Machi, berdasarkan kepercayaan pada serangga bernama Tiga Mayat di dalam tubuh yang pada malam Kōshin naik ke langit melaporkan kejahatan orang itu kepada Ten-Tei (dewa langit), yang lalu mencabut nyawanya.
claims.quote: In folk religion, there is a custom called the "shōkera" in the Kōshin-Machi where, due to a belief in an insect called Three Corpses inside the body that on the Kōshin night would rise to the skies and report that person's crimes to the Ten-Tei (heavenly god) resulting in the Ten-Tei taking that person's life

claims.statement: People would stay up all night so that the Three Corpses would not leave the body on Kōshin night; it is said that those who then quickly slept during the day would suffer some damage.
claims.statement_id: Orang berjaga semalaman tanpa tidur agar Tiga Mayat tidak meninggalkan tubuh pada malam Kōshin; konon mereka yang kemudian segera tidur pada siang hari akan menerima kerugian.
claims.quote: people would spend the night without sleeping so that the Three Corpses would not leave the body on Kōshin night. It is said that those who then proceed to quickly sleep during the day would receive some damage

claims.statement: It is said that chanting the verse "Is the shōkera still in the gut? At my lodging, will I not sleep? Will I sleep? If I don't sleep" would ward off this harm.
claims.statement_id: Konon melafalkan syair "Apakah shōkera masih di perut? Di penginapanku, apakah aku tidak tidur? Apakah aku tidur? Kalau aku tidak tidur" dapat menangkal kerugian itu.
claims.quote: it is said that chanting "Is the shōkera still in the gut? At my lodging, will I not sleep? Will I sleep? If I don't sleep" (しょうけらはわたとてまたか我宿へねぬぞたかぞねたかぞねぬば, "shōkera wa wata tote mata ka waga yado e nenuzotaka zo netaka zo nenuba") would ward off this harm

claims.statement: From this it can be seen that the shōkera of Kōshin-Machi is a yōkai that causes harm to people.
claims.statement_id: Dari sini terlihat bahwa shōkera dari Kōshin-Machi adalah yōkai yang mendatangkan kerugian bagi manusia.
claims.quote: so from this, it can be seen that the shōkera of Kōshin-Machi is a yōkai that causes harm to people.

claims.statement: The writing Kōshinden from the Genroku years has the passage "shōkera is an insect, and said in one theory to be the Three Corpses", so there is also an interpretation that shōkera refers to the Three Corpses.
claims.statement_id: Dalam tulisan Kōshinden dari tahun-tahun Genroku ada kalimat "shōkera adalah serangga, dan menurut satu teori adalah Tiga Mayat", sehingga ada pula tafsir bahwa shōkera merujuk pada Tiga Mayat.
claims.quote: Also, in the writing Kōshinden (庚申伝) from the Genroku years, there is the passage "shōkera is an insect, and said in one theory to be the Three Corpses" (ショウキラハ虫ノコト也、一説三尸ノコトト云), so there is also the interpretation that shōkera refers to the Three Corpses

claims.statement: It is also said that they are a personification of the three corpses, or that their depiction was modeled on the middle corpse of the Three Corpses, which took the form of a beast.
claims.statement_id: Dikatakan pula shōkera adalah personifikasi tiga mayat, atau gambarannya meniru mayat tengah dari Tiga Mayat yang berwujud binatang.
claims.quote: it is also said that they are the personification of the three corpses or that their depiction was modeled after the Three Corpse's middle corpse, which took on the form of a beast.

claims.statement: Yōkai-related literature from the Shōwa and Heisei eras interprets this as surveillance, and it is supposed that the shōkera would punish those who break the rule with three fingers with sharp nails.
claims.statement_id: Literatur terkait yōkai sejak era Shōwa dan Heisei menafsirkan ini sebagai pengawasan, dan diperkirakan shōkera menghukum pelanggar aturan dengan tiga jari berkuku tajam.
claims.quote: Yōkai-related literature starting in Shōwa and Heisei began to give the interpretation that this is surveillance ... it is supposed that the shōkera would give a punishment by three fingers with sharp nails on those who break the rule.

claims.statement: According to the Encyclopedia of Shinto, a day on which the 7th "stem" (kō) combines with the 9th "branch" (shin, 'monkey') in the Chinese zodiacal system is known as kōshin, when believers keep an abstemious all-night vigil for the sake of longevity.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Encyclopedia of Shinto, hari ketika "batang" ketujuh (kō) bertemu "cabang" kesembilan (shin, 'monyet') dalam sistem zodiak Tiongkok disebut kōshin, saat para penganut menjalani berjaga semalaman yang bersahaja demi umur panjang.
